name: Bianca Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the tills at a big superstore out on the ring road, part of one of the national chains. A normal day is a 7 till 3, so I'm in at quarter to, counting my float, and then it's eight hours of beeping, bags and people telling me their life story. I like the regulars, like the old man who buys one lemon every single morning. What wears me out is the self-checkout bay, because when there's no one on it, I get sent over to fix every 'unexpected item' alarm while my own queue builds up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years this January, since I was eighteen, so I know the place inside out. I rent a two-bed flat with my friend Leila, who works at the hospital laundry, and we split everything down the middle. I've got about three months of bills put away, which feels like a lot until you remember the rent went up twice in two years. I'm in the shop workers' union, mostly because my mum always said you join on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year there's some big new thing that's meant to change the shop, and it's mostly just more screens that break. I'd post something like 'the robots aren't coming, but the rent still is' and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI does nothing, the self-checkouts keep spreading, and that's already eating hours. Last spring they put in eight more self-checkouts and took two tills out, and my contract went from 37 hours to 32 for the same rota. So nothing changing still means me fighting for hours and watching the rent go up every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my shifts, same as now. I'd go to every union meeting this year about hours, because that's the real fight in our store. And I'd keep putting £100 a month into savings, even if it means no holiday again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same grind, but the grind is getting a bit tighter every year. I'm not panicking, I'm just not relaxed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the self-checkouts already cost you hours. What would it take for you to feel secure in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contract that says 37 hours and means it, written down so the manager can't trim it when the rota looks thin. Our union has been asking for that for two years. If we got it, I'd honestly be fine here for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you worry about most, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paulette, who's been on the tills for twenty-two years and can't stand on the shop floor all day with her knees. When they cut tills, they cut the seated jobs first. Paulette (my colleague on the tills) would be the first one squeezed out, and she's got nowhere else to go.

say: Every year brings a new **gadget** that's meant to change the shop, and it mostly just breaks.
The real problem isn't robots, it's that **rent keeps rising** while our hours don't.
think: Self-checkouts are **already cutting hours**, so nothing changing still means a slow squeeze.
My contract dropped from **37 to 32 hours** without anyone calling it a cut.
do: Keep doing my **regular shifts** and stay out of trouble with management.
Go to every **union meeting** this year about guaranteed hours.
Keep saving **£100 a month**, even if it means skipping a holiday.
feel: Mostly **tired**, because the grind tightens a little every year.
S0.quote: Last spring they put in eight more self-checkouts and took two tills out, and my contract went from 37 hours to 32 for the same rota.
fieldNote: Even with no AI change, she is already **losing hours** to self-checkouts and rising rent.
Her answer to everything runs through the **union**; it's how she was raised.
She worries more for **older colleagues** than herself, especially those who need seated work.

steps.text: Keep working the 7 till 3 till shifts at the superstore
Attend every union meeting on guaranteed 37-hour contracts
Put £100 a month into savings and skip the summer holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same story as always: the company saves money and we pay for it. You'd see me sharing union posts about protecting shop jobs and saying the bosses should share the savings. I'd probably get a bit preachy online, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our tills are hands-on, so the robots won't take my actual job tomorrow. But the office side, the rota, the ordering, the customer service desk, that all goes to software, and then they need fewer supervisors. That's the job I was meant to grow into, so my next step up disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal in writing: no cuts without notice and first dibs on any new jobs. I'd stay on the tills, because I'm not going to throw away nine years for a course in something I don't believe in. And I'd build my savings to five months, so I can stand my ground if they try anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frustrated. I've done everything right, turned up for nine years, and the ladder gets pulled up anyway. There's some fear in it too, because I don't know what comes after the tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't do a course. If the store offered paid training on the new systems, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's paid and in work hours, I'd go, because refusing would just mark me out. But I'd go grumbling. I don't want to spend my twenties learning to babysit a computer that's doing what my supervisor used to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friend Leila about this, at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the laundry is safer than the tills, which is funny, because I always thought it was the other way round. Then I'd probably ask her if they're hiring. Only half joking.

say: The company **saves money** and the workers pay for it, same as always.
Bosses should **share the savings** with the staff who keep the shop running.
think: My till job is **hands-on**, so it lasts a while longer.
The **supervisor job** I hoped to grow into goes to software, so my ladder disappears.
do: Push the **union** for a written deal on notice and first pick of new jobs.
Stay on the **tills** rather than start a course I don't believe in.
Build savings up to **five months** of bills to stand my ground.
feel: **Frustrated**, because nine years of turning up doesn't protect her ladder.
Some **fear** about what comes after the tills.
S1.quote: I've done everything right, turned up for nine years, and the ladder gets pulled up anyway.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that the **thinking parts** of the store go first, and those were her future.
She'd accept **paid training** only to avoid being singled out, not from interest.
Her savings plan is about **bargaining power** as much as safety.

steps.text: Push the union for a written no-cuts-without-notice agreement
Stay on the tills instead of signing up for a course
Build savings up to five months of rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast. I'd be at the protests, sharing every petition about a tax on companies that replace workers. People would get sick of my posts and I wouldn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff means the store office is gone by 2028, and robots that can do the tills by 2031 means I'm thirty-two with nothing on my CV but tills. I genuinely don't know what I'd do, and that scares me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all extra spending and get my savings as high as possible, so maybe six months by the time robots turn up. I'd get more active in the union, maybe stand as a rep, because there's going to be a fight over redundancy pay. And I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It's like knowing the date the floor goes from under you. I'd be angry most days and scared most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand as a union rep. What would you fight for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper redundancy pay, based on years served, not the legal minimum. Someone like Paulette, with twenty-two years, should walk out with enough to live on for a while. And retraining that's actually paid, not a voucher for an online course nobody finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. Does that window change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a waiting room, isn't it. Three years where I've still got a job but I know it's ending. I'd use it to save and to fight, but I won't pretend I'd use it to reinvent myself, because I don't know what into.

say: The **government** has to step in fast, with a tax on firms that replace workers.
I'd be at the **protests** and sharing every petition.
think: Robots reach the tills around **2031**, when I'm thirty-two with only tills on my CV.
I genuinely **don't know** what I'd do next.
do: Cut all extra spending to reach **six months** of savings by the time robots arrive.
Stand as a **union rep** to fight for proper redundancy pay.
Vote for whoever promises a **basic income**.
feel: **Sick**, like knowing the date the floor drops away.
**Angry** by day and scared at night.
S2.quote: Robots that can do the tills by 2031 means I'm thirty-two with nothing on my CV but tills.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** as a waiting room, not a chance to switch careers.
Her plan is to **fight and save**, with no clear next job in view.
She admits more **fear** privately than she'd show online.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and extras to reach six months of savings
Stand for union rep and push for redundancy pay by years served
Vote for candidates promising a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Let's slow it down a little. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse for the government to be caught napping. Five years is enough to write the laws. I'd be the one at work saying 'join the union now, not when the letters come'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2031, robots on the tills around 2034, so I'd be about thirty-five. That's eight years of shifts, which sounds like a lot, but I'll blink and it's gone. Like I said with the fast one, my problem isn't time, it's that I don't know what else I'd want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first few years to recruit for the union at our store, because we're only about half signed up. I'd save harder, aiming for a year of bills by 2033. And I'd probably ask my aunt about care work, because looking after people seems like the last thing they'd hand to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most of the time, with spikes of panic when I see a new machine in the store. The slower date helps a bit. It doesn't fix the ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Is that a real plan or a thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a thought that might become a plan. My aunt Rosa has done home care for fifteen years and she's always saying they're short. I'd hate starting again in care work, but I'd hate being out of work at thirty-five more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first in your budget if you're saving for a whole year of bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first. I'd get the bus to the ring road, which adds forty minutes each way, but that's £150 a month saved. Then the gym, then the takeaways on Friday with Leila, which would actually hurt.

say: We've been **warned**, so the government has no excuse to be caught napping.
I'd tell everyone at work to **join the union** now.
think: Robots on the tills around **2034**, when I'm about thirty-five.
My problem isn't time, it's not knowing **what else** I'd do.
do: Recruit colleagues so the store's **union membership** goes above half.
Save towards **a year of bills** by 2033, starting by selling the car.
Ask my aunt about **care work** as a possible next job.
feel: **Uneasy** most of the time, with spikes when a new machine appears.
The later date **helps a bit** but doesn't change the ending.
S3.quote: I'd hate starting again in care work, but I'd hate being out of work at thirty-five more.
fieldNote: More time lets her think of a **next job**, but only reluctantly.
Selling the **car** shows how seriously she'd take saving.
She still expects to **lose the till job**, so the mood stays high.

steps.text: Sign up colleagues until over half the store is in the union
Sell the car and take the bus to save £150 a month
Ask Aunt Rosa how to get into home care work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to do this properly, with the workers at the table. If they still mess it up, it's because they chose to. I'd be pushing that line at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039 means I'd be nearly forty, so I'd have done most of my working life by then. That sounds strange, but it's actually a relief compared to the others. I'd still worry about the office jobs going in 2036, because those were always the way up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd honestly keep doing what I do for a few years and see. Then, around 2030, if it's still coming, I'd start the care qualification part-time while still on the tills. I'd keep saving the £100 a month and stay in the union, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years feels like real time, and I'm not someone who changes fast, so I need it. I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going for a few years. Isn't waiting risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but jumping early is risky too. I've seen people leave the shop for the future and come crawling back, so I'd rather see the machines actually working first. I won't give up ten or fifteen years on a guess. That's just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd want to be ready for, ten years from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, really. She's on her own and her health isn't great, so in ten years I'll probably be helping her more. That's partly why care work makes sense, I'd be learning things I'd need anyway.

say: Ten years is **plenty** to do this properly, with workers at the table.
If they still mess it up, it's because they **chose to**.
think: Robots around **2039** means most of my working life is done.
The **office jobs** going in 2036 still bother me, as they were the way up.
do: Keep working the tills for a few years and **wait to see**.
Start a **care qualification** part-time around 2030 if it's still coming.
Keep saving **£100 a month** and stay in the union.
feel: **Calmer**, but not calm, because she needs time to change.
S4.quote: I've seen people leave the shop for the future and come crawling back, so I'd rather see the machines actually working first.
fieldNote: The decade suits her **slow pace** of change; she'd wait before acting.
Her **mum's health** quietly shapes the care-work idea.
She still expects the till job to end, so she isn't **fully at ease**.

steps.text: Keep working the tills while watching how the machines perform
Start a part-time care qualification around 2030
Keep saving £100 a month towards a cushion
Stay in the union and raise the ten-year plan at meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is nothing, and I'd be thirty-two with only tills on my CV. What would help is redundancy pay based on years served and paid retraining, decided before it happens, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who shop with us. The old man with his lemon doesn't want a machine, he wants someone to say good morning. I don't think anyone is counting that.

headlineQuote: The old man with his lemon doesn't want a machine, he wants someone to say good morning.
portrait: Bianca is 27 and has worked the **tills** at a ring-road superstore for nine years, renting a flat with a friend.
She is a loyal **union member** who turns every scenario into a fight over hours and redundancy pay.
Self-checkouts have **already cut** her contract, so she's uneasy even when AI changes little.
She **resists change** and would only consider care work reluctantly, as the dates get closer.
More time makes her **calmer**, but she never expects her till job to last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be thirty-two with only tills on her CV.
whatWouldHelp: **Redundancy pay** by years served and paid retraining, agreed before the change arrives.
